processing: A cultivar rather than a method: the leaf is suited to black tea, green tea and pu-erh, and each follows its own usual processing.
harvest_season: An early-budding variety; spring is the usual prized picking, as with other Yunnan large-leaf tea.
appearance_dry: As raw pu-erh the thick, very large leaves dry into broad, dark strands, typically with visible tips.
appearance_liquor: As raw pu-erh, typically a clear golden yellow.
appearance_wet: Very large, long-elliptical leaves, thick and supple.
taste_profile: This is a plant rather than a finished tea. Raw tea from Mengku is described as sweet, fragrant and vigorous, less smooth than some other Yunnan areas.

brewing.notes: These figures suit it made as raw pu-erh. The leaf is bulky, so weigh it instead of judging by eye, and keep early steeps short.

vintage_note: Sold under village names or simply as Mengku tea more often than as a variety. As pu-erh it goes by harvest year, young cakes first and aged ones with the age stated; as black or green tea it follows the usual current-year pattern of those classes.
description:
Mengku Dayecha, also called the Shuangjiang Mengku variety, is the large-leaf tea plant of Mengku Town in Yunnan, and a national improved variety in China. Its stated home is Bingdao, the village whose name now sells some of the costliest pu-erh.

It is seed-propagated, a tall early-budding tree with a clear trunk and very large leaves that lie flat or droop. It is suitable for black, green and pu-erh teas, so the plant alone tells you little about what is in the cup.

Mengku tea in general is known for thick, broad leaves, strong fragrance and vigour. Expect force and sweetness in raw pu-erh from this plant, and treat short steeps as the main brewing rule.

Since the plant is grown widely, the name is no promise of origin. Besides southwestern Yunnan it is planted at scale in Sichuan, Guizhou, Guangdong, Guangxi, Hainan and Hunan. When a label says Mengku large-leaf, ask where the garden actually is.
history:
The variety traces to Bingdao in Mengku, Shuangjiang County. From there it spread through the tea counties of southwestern Yunnan and was later introduced to other southern provinces.

In 1985 China's national crop variety committee recognised it as a national variety. Little is documented about who selected it or when.
